item.title: Every ED Is Raising Pay, So Why Can't Anyone Find Staff? (Part 2): Patients Can't Get Admitted, and Money Can't Buy People Back
item.description: This is Part 2. Part 1 is here. That post worked out three things that run against intuition: the number of board-certified emergency physicians who actually left the ED is not as large as the media claimed (72, not 139); ED patient volume has not particularly grown either: total visits still haven't returned to pre-pandemic levels today, and what changed is the mix inside; and it's not that everyone rushes to the ED with every little ailment: looking at the five-level triage as a whole, the share of low-acuity patients hasn't gone up, and has actually dipped slightly.

item.title: Every ED Is Raising Pay, So Why Can't Anyone Find Staff? (Part 1): The Misreported Number, and a Patient Population That Got Swapped Out
item.description:
This is Part 1. The piece comes in two installments: Part 1 covers "why people are leaving" and "whether there really are more patients"; Part 2 covers "why patients can't get admitted," and "why every hospital is raising pay and still can't find anyone."

On the ground: is the ED broken, or just busy?

Night shift hands off, day shift takes over. The moment sign-out ends, I already have 10 to 15 patients who are boarding or still have nowhere to go.
